title: Infinitus has raised $100M+ to help patients get healthcare faster - and they're hiring
author: Katie Kirsch
raw_text:
There is an invisible industry that sits between an American patient and the treatment their doctor prescribes. 
Someone has to confirm what the patient’s insurance will actually cover. Someone has to get the insurer’s permission before treatment can start. Someone has to enroll the patient in financial assistance and follow up on refills. So every year, millions of patients leave the doctor’s office with a prescription they never start. Not because medicine failed them - but because the healthcare system did.
Almost all of this still works the way it did in 1995 - someone at a pharmacy or hospital grinding through hold queues, fax machines, portals, and paperwork, one patient at a time. That labor is baked into what every American pays for healthcare, and it’s why treatment that should start in days sometimes takes weeks.
Infinitus
 was founded to help close this gap - and make healthcare access, adherence, and affordability easier than ever.
Watch the full podcast episode by scrolling to the end of the article.
The founding story
Ankit Jain
 first came up with the idea for Infinitus while at Google, in 2019. At the time, Google was demoing Duplex, an AI that could make calls - like to book dinner reservations at a restaurant. He mentioned this to his wife, who works in healthcare. Her reaction: “You have this incredible technology that can make phone calls on someone’s behalf - and it sounds like it can be used for a 
lot
 more than just booking restaurants.”
Ankit was inspired to reach out to a longtime friend and collaborator, 
Shyam Rajagopalan
 - a systems architect who had built high-throughput infrastructure at Snap and Google and designed CPUs at MIPS and NVIDIA earlier in his career. The two of them decided to run a test, to see if they could apply this new conversational AI technology to a much more complicated space: healthcare.
Ankit and Shyam called UnitedHealthcare and recorded a robotic voice saying, “Hi, this is Eva calling on behalf of Bruce Willis, and I’d like to collect benefits.” The first agent hung up immediately - but the second one answered every question “Eva” asked, before eventually saying, “Sorry, Bruce Willis isn’t a patient in our registry.”
That was when it clicked - this could work. 
Infinitus
 was born.
The technology
Infinitus revolves around one of the “least forgiving” interfaces in software - a live conversation, where there is no time to think, and no undo button.
If the AI takes two seconds too long, the person on the other end says “hello?” and hangs up. If it gets a coverage detail wrong, a patient waits longer for treatment. And these conversations can run past an hour, with hundreds of back-and-forth exchanges, which is more than most models can reliably handle by themselves.
To resolve this, Infinitus is built with the following:
A patent-pending Agent Response Control (ARC), which dynamically determines how tightly an AI agent's responses should be controlled during a conversation
A map of how every insurer actually operates, built from millions of real interactions - including which number to call, how each phone tree runs, and what each plan covers
A real-time pipeline - where turning speech into text, deciding what to do, and speaking back all happen seamlessly in milliseconds
What they’re building next
What Infinitus is building 
next
 is an agent that stays on a patient’s case for months, across channels – and this is opening up exciting new technical challenges for the team to tackle.
Much of the foundation already exists. Every interaction getting traced, scored, and fed back into the system, so the stack gets smarter with use. A workflow layer coordinating agents across a patient’s case, deciding what happens next and when a person needs to step in. Voice, chat, and SMS all running on the same core, so a conversation can move between channels without losing anything. Safety rules computed per customer and per regulation, checked in real time inside every conversation. A model-agnostic AI layer that picks the right voice, speech, and language model for the moment, instead of locking the whole system to one vendor. Memory that carries a patient’s context across calls, programs, and time. A quality system that grades and improves itself through constant simulation, evaluation, and optimization. And soon, AI agents and workflows adapting each patient’s journey in real time.
The results
Infinitus is now supporting over half of the Fortune 50 healthcare companies. Their agents have handled more than 350 million healthcare interactions and 10 million calls - saving countless hours for patients and providers.
This year, Infinitus’s AI beat human benchmarks by more than 18% on many tasks; over 90% of patients have rated the interactions positively; and admin costs are getting cut by up to 30%. Fast Company named Infinitus one of the world’s most innovative companies of 2025, and Andreessen Horowitz led the company’s $51.5M Series C, bringing the team’s total funding to $102.9M.
What it’s like to work at Infinitus
Infinitus is a flat organization that “doesn’t do titles.” There are no managers, senior managers, directors, or VPs.
If you’re an individual contributor, your title is a “member of X team.” If you lead a few people, you’re the descriptor of what you lead, with the word lead. (For example, Ankit himself carries the title of “Company Lead” rather than CEO. His co-founder’s title is “Technology Lead.”)
The team follows five main principles that they call “CODES”:
C
ustomer-obsessed
O
ptimistic realists
D
isagree and commit
E
ngage employees
S
ee-say-do – own the problem, don’t just spot it
In the hiring process, Ankit personally interviews everyone.
 He looks for people who have agency and don’t wait to be told what to do - they just step up and do it. People who have urgency and a sense of fearlessness, and who enjoy being thrown curve balls and figuring it out.
Ankit says the best part of his job is “watching people step into work they didn’t think they were ready for, and rise to the occasion anyway.”
The team is based in San Francisco - where the engineering, product, and design teams work in the office three days per week. The GTM and operations teams are spread across the country, serving customers where they are.
Open roles
Infinitus is hiring across the board. These are the team’s P0 roles right now:
Forward Deployed Engineer
 (SF / NYC) - Embed directly with Infinitus’s most strategic customers to drive transformational AI adoption.
AI full stack engineer
 (SF) - Design, build, and scale AI-powered, user-facing products that make Eva’s healthcare interactions more intelligent, intuitive, and reliable

title: Astranis just raised $450M to build the world's most advanced satellites for high orbits
author: Katie Kirsch
raw_text:
For decades, everyone building broadband constellations was racing to put thousands of satellites into low Earth orbit (LEO). Fewer people were focused on geostationary orbit (GEO), in part because GEO was expensive, complex, and time-intensive to build for. This was a missed opportunity to serve these strategic higher orbits.
Twenty-two thousand miles up, GEO and other higher orbits serve governments and enterprises that require dedicated and resilient infrastructure for communications, monitoring, mobility, and defense applications. Historically, the industry either built shared capacity satellites for LEO - or enormous, over-engineered, spacecraft that took years to build.
 John Gedmark
 bet it could be done far faster.
John grew up in Kentucky and always had a passion for aerospace and satellites. In college, he led Purdue’s chapter of SEDS - “Students for the Exploration and Development of Space” - and met 
Ryan McLinko
, who was running MIT’s chapter. This was back in 2006, nearly a decade before they would co-found Astranis together.
John went on to receive his Masters in Aerospace Engineering from Stanford University, and cofound and run the Commercial Spaceflight Federation; Ryan built cubesats at Planet Labs and flight control systems for Sierra Nevada’s Dream Chaser after interning at SpaceX and the United Launch Alliance. In 2015, Astranis was founded to build advanced spacecraft to connect, secure, and protect commercial and national security interests, starting in GEO.
Today, Astranis is the first company to mass-produce spacecraft for GEO, with five MicroGEO satellites operating on orbit and contracts spanning customers like Taiwan, Oman, NASA, and the U.S. Space Force, where Astranis is the prime contractor on multiple programs of record. The company just closed $450M in new capital, bringing total funding to more than $1.2B, and they have huge ambitions for what’s next - lead the Expansion Era of space, and build the infrastructure for every orbit beyond LEO.
The company operates out of SF’s historic Pier 70 and is hiring right now across the board. If you want to work on hardware that goes in geostationary orbit, the Astranis team would love to meet you.
Top 10 Open Roles

 - Help own planning and executing environmental test campaigns for components, subsystems, and spacecraft, working directly with production and engineering teams to drive hardware from design through qualification.
Senior Propulsion Manufacturing Engineer
 - You’ll be responsible for the production of advanced propulsion components, getting them assembled into a subsystem, and integrating that subsystem onto the vehicle.
Senior Radiation Effects Engineer
 - Define the environmental requirements, lead circuit-level mitigation designs, and oversee advanced testing to ensure Astranis’ electrical systems survive the harshest orbits.
Senior Harness Design Engineer
 - Own the design of the wire harnesses that keep the spacecraft alive on orbit, translating electrical architecture into manufacturable, flight-reliable harness designs built to survive launch and the full mission life in geostationary orbit.
Senior Product Security Engineer (Applications)

title: Applied Intuition just launched Dana - a new way to build physical AI - and they're hiring
author: Katie Kirsch
raw_text:
“
Put intelligence on a billion machines
.”
That’s the ambition of 
Qasar Younis
 and 
Peter Ludwig
, the co-founders of 
Applied Intuition
 - a physical AI company working across industries - including trucking, construction, mining, and defense.
If they succeed, intelligence won’t just live on our phones and laptops - it will become part of the physical infrastructure of everyday life. Roads that are safer. Supply chains that are more durable. Farms that produce more with fewer resources. Mines that operate around the clock without putting workers at risk. Machines that continuously learn, adapt, and work together to make the physical world safer, more productive, and more resilient.
Applied Intuition
 was co-founded in 2017 by Younis and Ludwig, who both lived in the shadow of the auto industry while growing up outside Detroit. Younis studied engineering at the General Motors Institute of Technology Institute (now Kettering University), then spent his first seven years as an automotive engineer at GM and Bosch. He later went to Harvard Business School, founded a startup that got acquired by Google, and became the COO of Y Combinator.
At Google, he met Ludwig, whose father and grandfather had spent their careers at GM. Ludwig worked on Android Automotive while at Google, and he and Younis initially explored a self-driving startup after leaving. But they ultimately decided - instead of building self-driving vehicles, they would sell the simulation and tooling that other self-driving companies and automakers needed to build autonomous vehicles safely. This was the beginning of Applied Intuition.
Today, 18 of the top 20 global automakers and major U.S. Department of Defense programs run on Applied Intuition’s tools and infrastructure, operating systems, and autonomy stack. Last year, the company closed a $600M Series F at a $15B valuation, with Marc Andreessen on the board from day one, bringing total funding to nearly $1B. Just last week, the team 
launched Dana
, a new agentic platform for building, testing, deploying, and operating physical AI.
The team is headquartered in Sunnyvale, with offices spanning Ann Arbor, the D.C. Metro area, San Diego, London, Stuttgart, Munich, Stockholm, Bangalore, Seoul, and Tokyo - and they’re hiring across the board.
If you’re excited about moving AI into the physical world and building the infrastructure layer for intelligent machines - like cars, tanks, submersibles, and tractors - the team would love to hear from you.
Open Roles at Applied Intuition
Applied Intuition is hiring across the board. Here are some of the P0 roles right now, and why they matter:
Engineering Manager - Behavior
: Lead a team of engineers to architect and build next-generation behavior systems in complex environments across cars, trucks, mining & construction vehicles, and more.
Engineering Manager - Axion
: Lead the development of an all-domain autonomy toolchain spanning high-fidelity simulation, autonomy software, hardware/software integration, ML Ops, and human-machine interfaces.
Senior Firmware Engineer

Senior Software Engineer - ML Infrastructure
: Tackle complex data & compute problems across the company, working across the ML stack (dataset generation, training frameworks, compute, evaluation, and deployment).
Technical Program Manager - Core Autonomy
: Drive complex programs for the autonomy stack that runs across the L2+ passenger vehicle, L4 truck, and mining vehicle initiatives.

title: How Mintlify uses AI to build AI for devs
author: Dani Grant
raw_text:
Mintlify
 is powering agent-native documentation for over 20,000+ companies.
We wanted to know about the AI stack they use to operate internally - what automations let them move fast. So, we sat down with CEO 
Han Wang
 and asked him to walk us through every important agent and AI workflow they use inside Mintlify.
Here’s what we heard:
1. Agents that take support tickets → fixes in prod
Mintlify built a system that ingests every customer support ticket, identifies if it’s about an issue, and if so, assigns it to a coding agent to fix.
How it works:
An AI support agent (they use 
Parahelp
) responds to incoming support tickets in their helpdesk (they use 
Plain
)
A Slack integration pushes every new support ticket to Slack, too
A background coding agent (they use 
Replicas
) reads every Slack message and uses the Linear MCP to create tickets for anything actionable
The Linear Agent auto ingests every incoming ticket, and assigns Claude Code to all bug tickets
Claude Code takes a first pass automatically and submits a PR
Two AI code reviewing agents (Cursor BugBot and 
Greptile
) review every PR and give a confidence score
Engineers do the final review, run tests and hit merge when tests pass
Mintlify says this helps the team ship faster and reduce the time between a customer-reported issue and a production fix.
2. Design prototyping
Mintlify’s design team wanted to unblock engineers to run quickly on discrete features so they can ship at the speed of good ideas, and so that the design team gets to spend their time working on more high leverage, longer-term research and work.
They realized a lot of vibe coding platforms are good enough at creating a first pass at designing basic features – enough that a seasoned designer can look at the prototype, point out a couple changes and let engineers run. They set up both Lovable and Replit with the Mintlify design system so that the engineering team can prototype new features quickly in either platform.
When building a new feature, an engineer drops the Slack thread where the feature is discussed into Replit or Lovable for a quick prototype, and send the result to designers for a gut check & any edits.
3. A knowledge retrieval agent
Mintlify also wanted a knowledge agent to unblock anyone in the org when a question arises. So, they built a knowledge base agent with access to Notion + Google Drive + meeting notes + Slack + emails + codebase. When anyone has a question, they just at mention the KB agent in Slack.
It’s a simple idea, but it can make a huge difference in how much deep work gets done. Fewer people get interrupted, and people get unblocked faster.
This one is actually running on their 
own platform
 - they offer a shared memory layer that pulls in all internal code and communication and creates a sort of knowledge runtime for internal agents.
4. The CEO’s personal agent
Han built himself a “Han agent”, inspired by personal agents like OpenClaw. 
The Han agent has access to all the tools he uses, and is available right in Slack. So instead of switching contexts to read/write to any app, he just asks the Han agent to do things for him right from Slack.
How it’s built: 
Gumloop
 + integrations to all the tools.
5. Email agent
This one helps the team spend less time in emails, more time producing work, while still being highly responsive.
It checks emails every morning and marks spam or unimportant messages as read. It auto-forwards any emails that need to be routed to another team member automatically. For every real email, it drafts a response using past emails and the internal knowledge base.
How it’s built: Gumloop + email/Slack integrations
6. Morning sales brief
Every morning, this agent sends a rundown of all customer conversations and in-process deals.
How it’s built: Claude Cowork cron job using MCPs from Salesforce, 
Granola
, and 
Attention
 to pull customer conversations and pushes to Slack
7. The weekly intel agent
Each week it compiles what customers, partners, and adjacent companies shipped, then drops the roundup in a channel.
How it’s built: a vibe-coded script on a cron job, calling the Claude API with deep-research tools attached.
 The full stack
Coding: Claude + Cursor.
Design: Replit + Lovable.
Personal-agents: 
Gumloop
Tickets: 
Replicas
 (routing to Linear) + Linear agent (assign to Claude) + Claude (create PR) + Cursor/
Greptile
 (review PR)
Orchestration: Slack (interface) and 
Temporal
 (durable workflows).
Finally, Mintlify’s agent vs hire framework
Not everything is an agent. The team is still growing and actually 3xed in size last year. Here’s Han’s framework…
For every new problem that arises, check:
Is this a problem that can be solved by automation/agent?
Is this a problem that can be solved by a process change?
If no & no, solve with headcount.

title: How 11x uses AI agents to build AI agents
author: Dani Grant
raw_text:
11x
 is building revenue agents to autonomously generate pipeline for customers - but that’s just the tip of the iceberg. What about how the 11x
 team uses AI 
internally
?
We sat down with CEO 
Prabhav Jain
 to map out the startup’s full internal AI stack - every agent and tool they use, so that the team can spend max time building for customers.
1. An agentic skill that turns deals away
When Prabhav transitioned from CTO to CEO, he made a rule - 11x is only selling to customers who will see a ton of value from 11x. This is counter to most companies’ approach, which is to sell to as many customers as possible. His reasoning: bad fit customers are not going to be happy customers, and they require a lot more energy to keep. When you narrow your customers to just your ICP, the team stays focused on building more value in the product, rather than appeasing bad fits that shouldn’t have been sold in the first place.
But at a people level, it’s hard to convince sales reps not to sell a deal. So he built a Claude skill that every sales rep uses.
It pulls in emails, call notes, and Slack messages exchanged with prospects. It considers industry-specific nuances and patterns from past successful customers. If it’s missing information it needs to evaluate the deal, it tells the rep what questions to ask the prospect. The agent then gives the rep a confidence score whether the customers is a fit or not - and reps only close deals that exceed a specific confidence threshold.
What we found interesting: they encoded a piece of 
judgment
 into something repeatable, and then used it to hold a line, which lets them move faster in the long term.
2. An agent that remembers the promises Sales made to customers
Customer happiness is expectations (what was promised during sales) minus reality (what the account team helps deliver).
To make sure every detail of what was promised upfront is communicated to the post-sale team, 11x built an internal agent.
Claude integrations pull every call from Granola, Slack, and email exchanged across the whole cycle. Then it generates a Notion doc and a kickoff deck.
The account and success managers who pick up the deal post-sale then know what matters to that exact customer and they can spend their time working on the right things for the customer.
3. “Lemmings” - codebase agents for the whole company
11x runs a company-wide fleet of internal codebase-read agents they call Lemmings. They work in the data and codebase on behalf of the non-engineering team. The non-engineering team just messages a Lemming in Slack, and can ask questions or ask for the Lemming to create a wide variety of customer-facing docs:
Create customer docs based on codebase, tailored to specific customer
Generate insights for a customer, and put into a polished doc
Debug and optimize a customer’s setup
Answer customer questions based on product and outcome data
Create decks for quarterly customer reviews
This is built with 
LangChain’s LangSmith Fleet
, which lets you describe in plain English a fleet of agents that work across your internal code and tools, and @mention them in Slack.
4. Testing agents that verify coding agents’ work
Like all startups, 11x uses coding agents heavily. But 11x also realized that as coding agents wrote more PRs, the bottleneck would move to verifying PRs.
So early on, they decided to invest heavily in building their own code harness. Here’s how the code harness verifies PRs created by agents:
Loads up a full virtual environment in Docker/Coder
Figures out what the PR is about and makes a test plan
Runs e2e automated tests in the virtual environment via Playwright
Runs an existing suite of regression tests
Puts evidence of the new feature working via screenshot in the PR
Has mock data that mimics production (including volume) and ensures performance efficiency doesn’t drop with any new PR
5. The agentic office of the CEO
Finally, Prabhav has built himself a fleet of personal agents that help surface the highest leverage information every day, all running on Claude Cowork scheduled jobs.
The first is a 
customer brief
, delivered via Slack DM each week. It ingests every customer call via the Granola MCP. This gives him a weekly update on what matters for customers right now.
The second is a 
meeting prep agent
 that reads email, Slack, Granola, conducts research and preps him for the next day’s meetings.
The third combs through his Slack every night and 
flags unresolved threads
. Resolution isn’t always explicit, it could be just an emoji reaction, or it could be in a different DM than the main discussion thread, so the agent has to reason.
A fourth is a 
weekly market pulse
. It pulls from the internet, and also from objections and competitors mentioned in that week’s deals in calls and emails. This gives him a pulse on what the field is seeing.
Final thoughts
Before Prabhav was the CEO of 11x, he was the CTO. He’s an engineer in the CEO seat during a time when a lot of people problems can be, well, engineered to solve.
As an aside, we asked Prabhav what it was like to go from 11x’s CTO to becoming CEO. “Intense,” he said and laughed, “but also fulfilling.”
It’s not an AI workflow, but he did give us the 4-step playbook that he used for anyone stepping into the role of CEO at an existing startup – and we thought we’d share it with you, as it’s relevant to any builder working to re-focus a startup:
Ruthlessly prioritize around a single focus: customer value
. Review everything the team is working on, if anything doesn’t tie back to customer outcomes, cut it.
Create the smallest, most senior team possible
. This part is hard and requires a lot of thoughtfulness around how you part ways with those who aren’t staying, but to steer a ship quickly, you need a small senior nimble ship.
Actually fire your bad customers
. Customers who are a bad ICP fit won’t get value or be happy, because you shouldn’t have brought them on in the first place. Narrow your customers to just your ICP. That way, you get to be 100% focused on building more value, not just putting energy into rocky customer deployments.
Do a tour of duty on every team.
 You don’t fully understand every function until you do it yourself - and as a new CEO, sometimes you need to get in the weeds.
